acceptanceCriteria.statement: The home screen presents exactly one primary request-access CTA above the fold, and every other action is visually subordinate.
A business visitor can understand that Stablebridge helps move between fiat and stablecoins without relying on unsupported claims about licences, corridors, rates, settlement times, or insurance.
The integrator journey remains reachable from home and leads to the developer overview without competing with request access as the main action.
On narrow mobile viewports, the integrator link collapses into a secondary menu while request access remains the dominant visible action.
The request-access flow supports empty, validation-error, and submitted states, and validation does not clear entered values.
Developer code samples stack vertically on mobile and only scroll horizontally within their own container.

accessibilityAndRecovery: Navigation destinations should be labeled in text wherever they are exposed, so icon recognition is never required for primary wayfinding.
The request-access form should preserve user input on error and surface field-level guidance near the problem fields.
On successful request access, the confirmation state should remain on screen long enough to confirm completion and preserve a clear path to developer information.
Mobile code samples must keep their scrolling behavior local to the sample container so page-level scrolling is not disrupted.
Primary action placement in the request-access form must remain reachable in a single-handed portrait grip, with the submit control placed in the bottom thumb zone.
assumptions: The exact visual system, typography, and color values are not specified in the brief, so implementation should choose a restrained palette consistent with the cited evidence while avoiding any claim of a branded palette.
The precise wording of labels and button text is not supplied, so copy should be written to match the brief without introducing unsupported product claims.
The structure of the secondary menu on mobile is unspecified beyond the required collapse behavior, so the menu pattern may be chosen as long as the developer path remains available and subordinate.

principles: Use a persistent navigation frame with labeled destinations so business visitors and integrators can orient themselves quickly across home and developer content.
Reserve the single strongest visual emphasis for the request-access path; all secondary navigation and developer paths must remain visually subordinate.
Structure content so the main page explains the service in business terms first, then reveals developer detail as a secondary path rather than a peer CTA.
Use bordered, low-elevation containers and restrained accent use to keep the interface readable and to avoid turning marketing content into competing chrome.
globalDirection.summary: Position Stablebridge as a business-first stablecoin on/off-ramp homepage that explains the value proposition above the fold, puts request access ahead of every other action, and keeps developer integration entry points available without competing for prominence.

accessibility: Pair each navigation icon with a visible text label where navigation is exposed to reduce icon ambiguity.
Keep the primary action visually dominant while using subdued styling for secondary links and menu items.
Use clear state feedback for success and error variants so form outcomes are readable without relying on color alone.
failureAndRecovery: If request access fails, keep the form context on screen and expose field-level errors near the relevant inputs.
If a submission succeeds, replace the form prompt with a confirmation state that preserves navigation to developer information.
If the integrator entry is hidden inside a narrow-viewport menu, ensure the menu label indicates a secondary path rather than competing with request access.
mobileRules: single primary action above the fold
integrator link collapses into a secondary menu on narrow viewports
screenBlueprints.summary: Responsive landing page for businesses that states Stablebridge’s role in moving between fiat and stablecoins, presents one primary request-access action above the fold, and keeps the integrator path available in secondary navigation.

accessibility: Keep integration information discoverable through explicit labels rather than icon-only navigation.
Use a container boundary around code samples so horizontal scrolling does not affect the full page.
Preserve page orientation cues so engineers can return from code to overview without losing their place.
failureAndRecovery: If code samples overflow on mobile, confine horizontal scrolling to the sample container only.
If the user arrives from the home page, retain a clear back path or home destination so the secondary journey can reverse cleanly.
If the overview contains multiple sections, keep each section distinctly labeled to avoid confusion between high-level explanation and implementation detail.
mobileRules: code samples stack vertically and remain horizontally scrollable only within their container
screenBlueprints.summary: Developer-facing overview page that presents integration information as a secondary destination from home, with content arranged for scanning and code samples contained so they remain readable within their own area.

accessibility: Place labels above fields so they remain visible during correction and re-entry.
Keep the submit action at the end of the form so decision time follows completion of the inputs.
Ensure validation states identify the specific field that needs correction rather than relying on a generic error banner alone.
failureAndRecovery: On validation error, preserve entered values and surface inline guidance adjacent to the failing field.
On submit success, confirm the request without forcing the user to resubmit or re-enter details.
If the keyboard covers lower fields on mobile, maintain access to the submit action by keeping it within the thumb zone and within the usable portrait grip.
mobileRules: primary submit action sits in the bottom thumb zone
required fields remain usable in a single-handed portrait grip
screenBlueprints.summary: Form flow for business teams requesting access, designed to be reachable from home and optimized for portrait mobile use with the submit control in the bottom thumb zone.

sourceDecisions.rationale: Retain the pattern of pairing navigation icons with visible labels so first-time visitors can decode destinations without guessing, while preserving spatial memory for returning users.
Adapt the idea of a stable navigation anchor so home and developer journeys stay oriented during scrolling, but keep it responsive rather than forcing a desktop-only rail on narrow screens.
Reserve the strongest accent for one primary action so request access stays visually dominant and secondary actions do not compete.
Use borders and rounded frames instead of shadows to separate sections and cards, which supports scanning without adding extra visual depth.
Place labels above inputs instead of relying on floating placeholders so the form remains legible during correction and re-entry.
Keep the developer path available from home as a secondary route rather than elevating it to equal weight with request access.
Reject icon-only navigation because the brief requires business visitors and integrators to understand destinations without guessing, and icon-only patterns depend too heavily on prior memory.
Reject layouts that give request access and developer exploration equal visual weight because the brief allows exactly one primary action above the fold.
Reject floating placeholders because the access form must stay readable during correction and re-entry, and placeholder-only labeling hides the field meaning once text is entered.
Reject drop-shadow-heavy containers because they introduce depth cues that compete with CTA hierarchy and make the page feel more layered than the brief supports.
